doc.title: Skitch Henderson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Milford, Connecticut, October 31, 1998

title: Steinway piano 199 and Horowitz
summary: The Steinway 199 concert grand Ruth bought, and Horowitz playing it for the children.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: I can imagine you’ve had to play some questionable pianos dating back to your Montana days, and I think it’s interesting that now you have this association with Steinway.

Well I always was the seventh son in the Steinway family. The B that’s behind me here was my NBC piano for years. And 199, the concert grand, which is adjacent, in the hierarchy of the days of Graffman, Catcham, Horowitz — oh I could name, I’ll leave the most important — Rubenstein, 199 was the most sought after concert grand for some strange reason. So much of it was a pain in the neck to the Steinway factory because Horowitz would take it to Omaha and then he’d suddenly forget to ship it back, he wanted to take it to Lincoln or someplace the next night or the next week. And they got so disgusted, that John Steinway said, “We’re going to take it out of inventory.” And when Ruth found that out she went quietly to him and said, “Can I buy it, we won’t tell anybody.” And it sits here. And it’s in pretty good shape. When at first my son was young, twelve, ten, twelve years old or something here at the farm once, and I used to have it in a studio. My wife has removed the studio, it’s her office now. But I had it in the studio over here. And I was always asking Horowitz, who was my neighbor, to come

over and play because I wanted to know where the piano should sit. We lived in barns you know. Where should the piano sit? But he never came. He always said, “I come Skitch, ya, I come.” Never came. One day we’re having dinner or lunch with some friends, and my son comes running up to where we were and he said, “There’s an old man playing your piano.” And it was Volodya, playing Chopin, for the kids. And they sat and listened. And that was 199. He was happy to have the reunion.
